name: Jerusalem
summary: A walled Old City holding the Western Wall, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the Al-Aqsa compound within a few hundred metres of each other. Bethlehem, the Dead Sea and Masada are day trips. Check current travel advice before planning, as the security situation changes.
seasonNote: Spring and autumn are mild; summer is hot and dry; winter can bring rain and occasional snow. Many sites close or change hours on the Sabbath (Friday evening to Saturday evening), Friday prayers and religious holidays.
arrival: Ben Gurion Airport is 50 km away; the fast train reaches Jerusalem's Yitzhak Navon station in about 25 minutes. Allenby Bridge links Jordan.
gettingAround: Walk the Old City; the light rail crosses the new city. Arab buses from Damascus Gate run to Bethlehem; tours reach the Dead Sea.
cashTip: Cards widely accepted; carry shekels for the souq, buses and tips.
foodTip: Hummus and falafel in the Old City, ka'ak sesame bread, and the stalls of Mahane Yehuda market.
buyTip: Armenian ceramics, olive-wood carvings, spices and za'atar.
baseArea: Near Jaffa Gate or the German Colony; East Jerusalem near Damascus Gate is cheaper

connections.note: Fast trains to Tel Aviv; not on the Sabbath.
Via the Allenby or Wadi Araba crossings; tours run.

items.name: Western Wall
items.summary: The surviving retaining wall of the Second Temple's platform, the holiest place where Jews can pray.
items.expect: Security checks; separate prayer sections for men and women; heads covered for men at the wall.
items.tip: Go on Friday at sunset to see the Sabbath welcomed, and book the Western Wall Tunnels tour.
items.why: The spiritual centre of Judaism.
flow: Enter via the Dung Gate or the Jewish Quarter.
Plaza, the wall, then the tunnels tour.
items.book: Tunnels tour a few days ahead

items.name: Church of the Holy Sepulchre
items.summary: The church built over the places Christians hold as Jesus's crucifixion, burial and resurrection, shared by several denominations.
items.expect: Long queues at the tomb; modest dress.
items.tip: Arrive at opening, around 5 am in summer, for a quiet visit to the Edicule.
items.why: The holiest site in Christianity.
flow: Walk the Via Dolorosa to the church.
Golgotha, the Stone of Anointing, then the tomb.

items.name: Haram al-Sharif and the Dome of the Rock
items.summary: The compound Muslims call al-Haram al-Sharif and Jews the Temple Mount, with Al-Aqsa Mosque and the golden Dome of the Rock.
items.expect: Non-Muslims may visit the courtyard only in limited morning and early afternoon hours through the Mughrabi Gate, never during prayers, and may not enter the mosques. It can close without notice.
items.tip: Check the day's visiting hours, dress modestly and bring no religious items.
items.why: The third holiest site in Islam and the holiest in Judaism.
flow: Queue at the Mughrabi Gate ramp by the Western Wall.
Walk the courtyard around the Dome.

items.name: Via Dolorosa and the Old City quarters
items.summary: The route of the Stations of the Cross through the Muslim and Christian Quarters, and the lanes of the Armenian and Jewish Quarters.
items.expect: Crowded souq lanes; Friday afternoon processions led by Franciscans.
items.tip: Walk the ramparts from Jaffa Gate for a view into all four quarters.
items.why: The Old City is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
flow: Start at the Lions' Gate.
Via Dolorosa, the souq, then the ramparts.

items.name: Mount of Olives
items.summary: A hill of ancient Jewish graves and churches, with the classic view over the Old City.
items.expect: A steep walk; go down rather than up.
items.tip: Taxi to the top at sunrise and walk down past the Garden of Gethsemane.
items.why: The best view of Jerusalem.
flow: Taxi to the viewpoint.
Walk down via Dominus Flevit to Gethsemane.

items.name: Yad Vashem
items.summary: Israel's Holocaust memorial and museum.
items.expect: Free; closed on Saturdays; not suitable for young children.
items.tip: Allow at least three hours and end at the Children's Memorial.
items.why: A profound and essential memorial.
flow: Light rail to Mount Herzl, then a shuttle.
History museum, then the memorials.

items.name: Church of the Nativity
items.summary: The basilica over the grotto that Christians venerate as the birthplace of Jesus, in Bethlehem in the West Bank.
items.expect: A checkpoint crossing; Israeli citizens may not enter Area A. Long queues for the grotto.
items.tip: Take Arab bus 231 from Damascus Gate, hire a local Palestinian guide, and see Manger Square and the Old City.
items.why: One of Christianity's holiest sites and a UNESCO World Heritage site.
flow: Bus from East Jerusalem, 30 minutes.
Church and grotto, Milk Grotto, then Manger Square.

items.name: Masada and the Dead Sea
items.summary: Herod's clifftop fortress above the Dead Sea, then a float in the saltiest water on earth at the lowest place on land.
items.expect: Very hot; climb the Snake Path before sunrise or take the cable car.
items.tip: Do Masada at dawn, then float at Ein Bokek and add Ein Gedi on the way back.
items.why: A UNESCO site and an experience found nowhere else.
flow: Tour or car, 90 minutes.
Masada at sunrise, Dead Sea float, Ein Gedi.

items.name: Mahane Yehuda Market
items.summary: Jerusalem's main market, with produce and bakeries by day and bars and restaurants by night.
items.expect: Packed on Thursdays and Friday mornings before the Sabbath.
items.tip: Try rugelach from Marzipan and the kubbeh soup stalls.
items.why: The liveliest place in the city.
flow: Light rail to Mahane Yehuda.
Graze by day, return for drinks at night.

items.name: Abu Shukri
items.summary: A long-running hummus house on the Via Dolorosa.
items.expect: Lunchtime only; closes when the hummus runs out.
items.tip: Order hummus with ful and fresh pita.
items.why: Often called the best hummus in the Old City.
flow: On El Wad Road near the fifth station.
Hummus, falafel and salads.

items.name: Machneyuda
items.summary: A loud, fun restaurant cooking from the market each day, known for its party atmosphere.
items.expect: Expensive and noisy; book ahead.
items.tip: Sit at the bar to watch the kitchen.
items.why: The restaurant that made Jerusalem a food city.
flow: Reserve.
Share small plates from the daily menu.

name: Tel Aviv · Jaffa
tagline: Beaches, Bauhaus and an ancient port
summary: A beach city of white Bauhaus buildings, cafés and nightlife, joined to the ancient port of Jaffa. Check current travel advice before planning.
seasonNote: Summers are hot and humid; beaches are warm from May to October. Shops and transport largely stop on the Sabbath.
arrival: Ben Gurion Airport is 20 km away; trains reach the centre in 15 minutes.
gettingAround: Walk or cycle (Tel-O-Fun bikes); the light rail and buses cover the rest.
foodTip: Sabich, shakshuka, hummus and modern Israeli restaurants; Carmel Market for street food.
buyTip: Design shops in Neve Tzedek and the Jaffa flea market.
baseArea: Near the beach between Gordon and Frishman, or Neve Tzedek

connections.note: Fast trains; not on the Sabbath.

items.name: Old Jaffa
items.summary: One of the world's oldest ports, with a stone old town, a clock tower and a flea market.
items.expect: Hilly lanes; the flea market is busiest on Fridays.
items.tip: Walk the beach promenade from Tel Aviv to Jaffa at sunset.
items.why: Thousands of years of history at the edge of a modern city.
flow: Walk or bike south along the promenade.
Clock tower, old town lanes, flea market.

items.name: Tel Aviv beaches and promenade
items.summary: A 14 km sandy coastline with lifeguards, beach bars and matkot paddle-ball players.
items.expect: Lifeguards from May to October; strong currents on red-flag days.
items.tip: Gordon and Frishman beaches for a classic day; Hilton Beach is surfers' and gay-friendly.
items.why: The city's everyday life happens on the beach.
flow: Pick a beach.
Swim, then a drink at sunset.

items.name: White City Bauhaus walk
items.summary: More than 4,000 white modernist buildings from the 1930s, the world's largest group of Bauhaus-style architecture.
items.expect: Self-guided or free walking tours from the Bauhaus Center.
items.tip: Walk Rothschild Boulevard and Bialik Street.
items.why: A UNESCO World Heritage site.
flow: Bauhaus Center on Dizengoff Street.
Bialik Street, then Rothschild Boulevard.

items.name: Carmel Market
items.summary: The city's main market of produce, spices and street food, beside the Yemenite Quarter.
items.expect: Busiest Friday mornings; closed on Saturdays.
items.tip: Eat in the lanes of the Yemenite Quarter behind it.
items.why: The best place to eat cheaply.
flow: Start at Magen David Square.
Walk the market, then the Yemenite Quarter.

items.name: Neve Tzedek
items.summary: The first Jewish neighbourhood built outside Jaffa, now boutiques and cafés in restored houses.
items.expect: Quiet and pretty.
items.tip: Finish at the old railway station, HaTachana.
items.why: The most charming streets in Tel Aviv.
flow: Shabazi Street.
Suzanne Dellal Centre, then HaTachana.

items.name: Tel Aviv Museum of Art
items.summary: A strong collection of Israeli and international art in a striking modern wing.
items.expect: Closed some weekdays; check hours.
items.tip: Go on a hot afternoon.
items.why: The country's leading modern art museum.
flow: Bus or bike.
Israeli art, then the European collection.

items.name: Abu Hassan
items.summary: A famous Jaffa hummus shop that closes when the day's pots run out.
items.expect: Shared tables and quick service; mornings to early afternoon.
items.tip: Order the masabacha, warm chickpeas over hummus.
items.why: Israel's best-known hummus.
flow: Dolphin Street, Jaffa.
Hummus and pita, no menu needed.

items.name: Sabich Frishman
items.summary: A tiny stand serving sabich: fried aubergine, egg and salads in pita.
items.expect: A queue at lunch.
items.tip: Ask for amba mango pickle.
items.why: The classic version of Tel Aviv's favourite sandwich.
flow: Corner of Frishman and Dizengoff.
Sabich to go.

items.name: Port Sa'id
items.summary: A buzzing open-air restaurant and bar by the Great Synagogue, from chef Eyal Shani's group.
items.expect: No bookings; lively crowd.
items.tip: Order the whole roasted cauliflower.
items.why: The essence of Tel Aviv's casual food scene.
flow: Allenby Street.
Small plates and drinks outside.

name: Haifa · Galilee
tagline: Bahá'í terraces, crusader Acre and the Sea of Galilee
summary: A port city climbing Mount Carmel, home to the Bahá'í World Centre's terraced gardens. Crusader Acre, Nazareth and the Sea of Galilee are all within an hour. Check current travel advice before planning.
seasonNote: Mild spring and autumn; hot summers; wildflowers in March and April.
arrival: Trains from Ben Gurion Airport and Tel Aviv take about an hour.
gettingAround: The Carmelit funicular climbs the hill; trains and buses reach Acre and Nazareth; a car is easiest for Galilee.
foodTip: Arab cuisine in Wadi Nisnas and the German Colony; knafeh in Nazareth; fish by the harbour in Acre.
buyTip: Spices and sweets in Acre's market.
baseArea: The German Colony or the Carmel Centre

items.name: Bahá'í Gardens and Shrine of the Báb
items.summary: Nineteen terraces of gardens descending Mount Carmel to the golden-domed Shrine of the Báb, the holiest Bahá'í place after Acre.
items.expect: Free; the full terraces only by guided tour from the top; modest dress.
items.tip: Join the free English tour from the upper terrace and walk down to the German Colony.
items.why: A UNESCO World Heritage site and one of the most beautiful gardens in the world.
flow: Bus to the top of the terraces.
Guided descent, then the shrine and the German Colony.

items.name: German Colony
items.summary: A boulevard of 19th-century Templer houses leading up to the Bahá'í Gardens, lined with restaurants.
items.expect: Lively in the evening.
items.tip: Walk it at dusk with the gardens lit above.
items.why: Haifa's best street for dinner.
flow: Ben Gurion Boulevard.
Walk up to the foot of the gardens.

items.name: Acre old city
items.summary: A walled crusader and Ottoman port with underground Knights' Halls, a tunnel and a lively souq.
items.expect: 30 minutes by train; busy at weekends.
items.tip: Buy the combined ticket for the Knights' Halls and Templars' Tunnel, and visit the Bahá'í gardens at Bahjí just north.
items.why: A UNESCO World Heritage site.
flow: Train to Akko.
Knights' Halls, the tunnel, the souq, then the harbour.

items.name: Nazareth and the Basilica of the Annunciation
items.summary: The largest church in the Middle East, over the place where Christians believe the angel Gabriel appeared to Mary, in an Arab city.
items.expect: Modest dress; the old market is quiet on Sundays.
items.tip: Walk the old market and have knafeh at Mahroum.
items.why: Jesus's hometown and a major pilgrimage site.
flow: Bus or car, 45 minutes.
Basilica, St Joseph's Church, the old market.

items.name: Sea of Galilee
items.summary: The lake of Jesus's ministry, with Capernaum, Tabgha and the Mount of Beatitudes on its shore.
items.expect: An hour by car; churches close at midday.
items.tip: Visit Capernaum, Tabgha and the Mount of Beatitudes in the morning, then lunch in Tiberias.
items.why: Central places of the Gospels in a lovely setting.
flow: Drive to the north shore.
Mount of Beatitudes, Tabgha, Capernaum, Tiberias.

items.name: Stella Maris and the Carmel cable car
items.summary: A Carmelite monastery over Elijah's Cave on the cliff top, reached by cable car from the beach.
items.expect: Small; open to visitors.
items.tip: Ride the cable car up from Bat Galim beach for the view.
items.why: The mother house of the Carmelite order.
flow: Cable car from Bat Galim.
Monastery, then down to Elijah's Cave.

items.name: Fattoush
items.summary: A cosy Arab restaurant and bar with a garden on the German Colony boulevard.
items.expect: Busy at weekends.
items.tip: Sit in the garden and share mezze.
items.why: The German Colony's favourite.
flow: Ben Gurion Boulevard.
Mezze, then grilled meats.

items.name: Wadi Nisnas
items.summary: Haifa's Arab quarter, with a market of falafel, bakeries and sweet shops among street murals.
items.expect: Busiest on Saturday mornings.
items.tip: Try falafel at Hazkenim and baklava from the sweet shops.
items.why: The heart of Haifa's Arab food culture.
flow: Walk down from the German Colony.
Market lanes and street art.

items.name: Uri Buri
items.summary: A celebrated seafood restaurant in an Ottoman house by Acre's lighthouse.
items.expect: Book ahead; a tasting menu of small dishes.
items.tip: Let chef Uri choose.
items.why: One of the best seafood restaurants in the region.
flow: Reserve.
Tasting menu after a day in Acre.
